chapter_theme: Madari returns from her river worship with news heard in the town; Kannaki, not finding her husband, presses for what people say, learns that he is called the thief of the palace anklet and that the guards have killed him, laments that the king's straying sceptre has made her a widow, and calls on the sun as witness, which answers that he is no thief and that fire will eat the city.

cast.role: Kovalan's wife, waiting in the herders' quarter for his return
Kannaki's husband, killed in Madurai as a thief
the aged herdswoman (ஆயர் முதுமகள்) who leads the kuravai and in whose house Kannaki lodges
the young herdswomen who danced the kuravai with Madari
the sun, whom Kannaki calls on as witness and whose voice answers her (the next kaathai opens என்றனன் வெய்யோன்)
the Pandya's guards who carry out the killing
the Pandya king of Madurai who had Kovalan killed (named here as மன்னவன், தென்னவன்)

silappathikaram:18:1-15.reading: Madari, who had gone to the long-flowing Vaigai with flowers, incense and garlands to worship Mal at the end of the kuravai, hurries back on hearing a stir in the town and stands without a word, while Kannaki, unable to find her husband, says her heart heaves like a forge's bellows and asks her friend what the strangers have been saying.
silappathikaram:18:1-15.nuance: The refrain form (a line, then its second half repeated as the next line with அன்றே turned to ஆயின், closing on 'what did they say, friend?') makes the dread grow through the repetition before any news is told. Madari's silence is itself the message: the poem has her come back with news and not speak it. Lines 8 to 10 play on சொல்லாடாள் and சொல்லாடும், and it is not certain whether they mean Madari's silence speaks to Kannaki or that Kannaki speaks while Madari is silent; the reading here takes the second.
silappathikaram:18:1-15.event: Madari returns from worship at the Vaigai having heard a rumour, and Kannaki, not finding Kovalan, asks her friend what people are saying.

silappathikaram:18:16-33.reading: Kannaki's refrain continues that she trembles at noon and suspects some treachery, and the answer comes that men say he was a thief who silently took an anklet from the king's palace and that the guards with ringing anklets set out to kill him; hearing it, she rises, falls like the moon dropping with the clouds to earth, and weeps, calling for her husband.
silappathikaram:18:16-33.nuance: The charge comes as hearsay: கள்வனாம் ('a thief, they say') is reported speech, and the line is repeated as the song form's refrain, so the town's word is heard twice before Kannaki falls. Her suspicion of வஞ்சம் (line 21) comes before the news and frames it as a deception. The answer does not name who tells it; the reading takes it as what the townsfolk said, carried by the friend.
silappathikaram:18:16-33.event: Kannaki hears that Kovalan was called the thief of the palace anklet and marked for death by the guards, and falls weeping.

silappathikaram:18:34-53.reading: Kannaki asks whether, now that the king has erred and his sceptre has strayed from right, she must waste away in grief like the women who lose their husbands to the pyre and keep the hard observances of widowhood, losing even her good name in this life; then she bids the kuravai girls listen and asks the sun, who knows all in the sea-girt world, whether her husband is a thief, and a voice answers that he is not, and that fire will eat this city.
silappathikaram:18:34-53.nuance: In each of the three stanzas the cause is the king's fault alone (மன்னவன் தவறிழைப்ப, with the sceptre that wanders with cruelty and has gone beyond straightness), though the narrator had closed the killing with the king's bent sceptre and Kovalan's former deed together (16:216-217), and Kannaki herself will later name ஊழ்வினை before the king (20:69). Her question sets her apart from the widows who bathe at the ghats and keep the observances: the form 'shall I perish like them?' prepares her refusal of that path. அறனென்னும் மடவோய் (line 41) can be read as an address to Dharma itself as a simpleton that has failed her, or as an address to a naive woman; the sense is uncertain. The voice is unnamed here (ஒருகுரல்); the next kaathai opens என்றனன் வெய்யோன், making it the sun's.
silappathikaram:18:34-53.event: Kannaki laments the king's wrong, calls the sun to witness whether her husband is a thief, and a voice answers that he is innocent and that fire will consume Madurai.

claims.claim: the king's sceptre has strayed from rightness, and the king's error is what has robbed her of her husband
the sun knows all that is done in the world and can bear witness to a man's innocence

links.note: The kuravai ends praising the Pandya's victorious drum and asking the god to remove the herd's distress; the woman who led it comes back from the river with news of the Pandya's guards killing an innocent man.
links.teaches: Set side by side, the herdswomen's blessing on the king's victory is overtaken within lines by the report of his injustice, so the rite meant to avert evil omens is shown failing at the very moment it is completed.

links.note: The townsfolk say Kovalan is a thief (கள்வனாம்); the sun's voice answers கள்வனோ அல்லன்.
links.teaches: The kaathai sets the hearsay of men, which the king acted on, against the testimony of the all-seeing sun, so the case against Kovalan is answered by a higher witness before it ever reaches the king's court.

links.note: The rumour says he stole an anklet from the palace; in the next kaathai Kannaki tells the women of the city that he was no thief and was killed for the price of her own anklet.
links.teaches: Kannaki turns the private news she received into a public counter-charge, correcting the one fact the rumour got wrong (whose anklet it was), which is the fact the trial will turn on.

links.note: The sun's voice says bright fire will eat this city; in the vow, the fire god appears and says he was ordered long ago to eat the city on the day it wronged the great pathini.
links.teaches: The burning of Madurai is announced twice by gods, first by the sun as witness and then by the fire as agent, so Kannaki's act fulfils a sentence already spoken from above rather than a private revenge.

links.note: Here Kannaki names only the king's error as the cause; before the king she says her husband came to the city driven by ஊழ்வினை.
links.teaches: In private grief Kannaki blames the king alone, but in court she joins karma to his fault, so the two causes the patikam names are shown held by one speaker at two moments, not only by narrator and character.

links.note: The queen of Bhoothapandiyan refuses the widow's life of alli food and the gravel bed and chooses the pyre; Kannaki asks whether she too must waste away like the widows who keep those observances.
links.teaches: Both widows refuse the observances of kaimmai, but the Sangam queen turns to the pyre while Kannaki turns to the sun and the king, so the epic moves the wife's refusal of widowhood from death beside the husband to a demand for justice.

gains.a: the lament gains the Sangam measure of what the widows' observances were and that a high-born wife could reject them
gains.b: the poem's choice between widowhood and the pyre gains a third way, a widow who rejects both to accuse the king

source_issues: Lineation: the kaathai shows 53 lines against the edition's printed last line 50; short rubric-like lines (ஆங்கு, அவள்தான், எல்லாவோ, சொன்னது:-, எனக் கேட்டு, காணிகா) are counted as lines here.
Line 27 repeats line 26 (கரையாமல் வாங்கிய கள்வனாம் என்றே): flagged and kept as the song form's refrain.
